reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A treatable neuronopathy: any child with progressive deafness plus a motor and sensory neuronopathy deserves an empirical trial of high-dose riboflavin

Caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the riboflavin transporter genes SLC52A2 (RFVT2) or SLC52A3 (RFVT3), inherited recessively; it encompasses the Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere and Fazio-Londe phenotypes

The biochemical profile can mimic multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenation deficiency (MADD), with an abnormal acylcarnitine pattern and organic aciduria, because flavin cofactors are needed for fatty-acid oxidation flavoenzymes
Features include sensorineural deafness, bulbar palsy, axial and limb weakness, sensory ataxia, optic atrophy and respiratory compromise
Plasma flavin levels may be low but can be normal, so a normal result does not exclude the diagnosis
High-dose riboflavin supplementation frequently stabilises or reverses neurological decline and normalises the MADD-like metabolites
Treatment should be started on clinical suspicion rather than deferred until genetic confirmation
The MADD-like biochemistry can be a helpful clue that points towards a riboflavin-responsive disorder
reference.pathophysiology: Riboflavin transporter deficiency is caused by impaired cellular uptake of riboflavin (vitamin B2) owing to loss-of-function variants in SLC52A2 or SLC52A3. Reduced riboflavin uptake depletes the flavin cofactors FAD and FMN, which are essential for many flavoenzymes, including the acyl-CoA dehydrogenases and electron-transfer flavoprotein of mitochondrial fatty-acid beta-oxidation. Cofactor deficiency therefore produces a secondary, riboflavin-responsive phenocopy of multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenation deficiency, with a corresponding acylcarnitine and organic acid signature, and drives neurodegeneration of cranial motor nuclei, anterior horn cells and the auditory and optic pathways. Because the underlying problem is cofactor delivery, supraphysiological riboflavin can restore flavoenzyme function and improve both the metabolic and neurological abnormalities.
additionalDifferentials: Genetic multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (glutaric aciduria type II)
Motor neurone disease and spinal muscular atrophy
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of SLC52A2 and SLC52A3
Plasma acylcarnitine profile and urine organic acids for a MADD-like pattern
Audiometry and brainstem auditory evoked responses
redFlags: Respiratory insufficiency from bulbar and diaphragmatic weakness
Rapidly progressive dysphagia with aspiration risk
Acute metabolic decompensation during catabolic illness
Progressive visual loss from optic atrophy
reference.prognosis: Without treatment the disorder is progressive and potentially fatal, but early high-dose riboflavin supplementation often halts and partly reverses neurological deterioration, making prompt recognition decisive for outcome.
pitfalls: Diagnosing genetic MADD and missing the riboflavin-responsive transporter defect
Withholding empirical riboflavin pending genetic results
Interpreting normal plasma flavin levels as excluding the diagnosis
Attributing the picture to an untreatable motor neurone disease
references: OMIM entries for SLC52A2 and SLC52A3
management: Start high-dose oral riboflavin supplementation empirically without awaiting genetic confirmation, as it frequently stabilises or reverses the neurological decline
Continue riboflavin lifelong to maintain flavin cofactor supply
Respiratory surveillance with ventilatory support for diaphragmatic weakness and hypoventilation
Audiological rehabilitation with hearing aids or cochlear implantation for sensorineural deafness
Nutritional support and safe-swallow assessment, with gastrostomy feeding for bulbar involvement
Physiotherapy, mobility aids and neurorehabilitation for the motor and sensory neuronopathy
Monitor the acylcarnitine and organic-acid profile for normalisation as an index of biochemical response
Genetic counselling with sibling testing and an empirical riboflavin trial for affected relatives, given autosomal recessive SLC52A2 or SLC52A3 variants
